#39612 triggered FLT#972 . In other words, hopscotch (#general > hopscotch: an interactive tool to bump Lean dependencies @ 💬 ) noticed that #39612 (which splits Mathlib.Topology.Algebra.Module.LinearMap without deprecating the module) broke FLT (which has a file containing the line import Mathlib.Topology.Algebra.Module.LinearMap). The hopscotch PR to FLT immediately pinpoints the problem (it explicitly links to #39612) so it was trivial to fix. In particular I am not complaining, I am just observing.

My understanding is that we usually make module deprecations in another PR other than the one where the module is deleted (although I can't remember why). Is that still the philosophy? Because if so then I can imagine more hopscotch PRs like this. My question is simply whether this is the system working as intended (and it's fine if it is as far as I am concerned, with my hopscotch privileges of course, because as I say hopscotch now makes these kinds of things very easy to diagnose and fix).
We've been doing it to make the file movements easier to see in the git history, but at this point I'm a bit skeptical that it's worth the hassle.
Sorry, it's also my fault, I completely forgot to open the deprecate_module PR

Anatole, it's been like 24 hours or something, so I wouldn't say that's your fault. The issue is that hopscotch is continually building against the latest Mathlib, whereas before we had a window (until the next monthly release) where downstream projects wouldn't be affected.

Something confusing is when the commit used for nightly testing falls between a pair of these PRs. I'd not mentioned it because this is pretty niche, but it did happen in CSLib a while back with a very opaque error message. (But then again, if you're using a nightly perhaps it's expected to come with some rough edges)

Jireh Loreaux said:

Anatole, it's been like 24 hours or something, so I wouldn't say that's your fault. The issue is that hopscotch is continually building against the latest Mathlib, whereas before we had a window (until the next monthly release) where downstream projects wouldn't be affected.

I think part of the issue is that a lot of downstream projects update Mathlib very frequently, use the release candidate toolchains, etc. so it's easy to not think about the monthly release as an atomic operation. Especially if you want to be able to distinguish between core and Mathlib breakage, this is somewhat necessary, but I try to be mindful that edge cases like this are a result and I personally don't want to put disproportionate pressure on Mathlib folks to consider them all.

Yeah, right now with FLT I am experimenting with daily bumps to mathlib current master via hopscotch and preliminary indications are that this is working super-well. Before hopscotch, I was doing weekly FLT bumps and then trying to figure out how to fix the two or three unrelated things which broke, but now I am getting really precise feedback with daily bot-generated PRs either of the form "FLT worked yesterday and still works today, here's the bump" or "FLT worked yesterday but this commit from < 24 hours ago broke it today, here is a partial bump and a link to the mathlib commit which broke it, to hopefully make it trivial to fix". The reason I'm raising this is that I am wondering whether this hopscotchian approach will become the new normal, and in that case we will have to decide whether the advantages of "deprecate with a second PR" (doesn't screw up github historydiff) outweigh the disadvantages. The particular disadvantage I am flagging here is "FLT gave an error which was trivial to fix instead of a warning which was trivial to fix" so in particular the disadvantage genuinely is tiny, but Chris' nightly testing example is perhaps more confusing.
Note that the GitHub history is not the worst part, it's the "Files changed" view during review.
A possible fix would be "we create the deprecation right before merging the PR" (automatically ? using a GitHub bot ?)

For nightly testing and releases I'd saying guaranteeing they share a bors batch is sufficient, but because hopscotch will check individual commits (not just the most recent of a batch that has a usual cache) this doesn't work. Even if they're adjacent commits, you'll still get the warning/error, right?

I'm not a hopscotch expert (just an early adopter) but I think it might be random. I think hopscotch bisects to figure out which commit broke the build so it all might be to do with how lucky you are with the power of 2 which divides the number of commits between the last time hopscotch ran and the commit which deleted the module without deprecating or whatever.

Anatole Dedecker said:

(automatically ? using a GitHub bot ?)

It'd be amazing if it can also automerge after CI! I currently have an open PR with module deprecations, and because of review bandwidth it's been 2 months since the modules were deleted, so I now wonder whether its moot to add deprecations.

Kevin Buzzard said:

I'm not a hopscotch expert (just an early adopter) but I think it might be random. I think hopscotch bisects to figure out which commit broke the build so it all might be to do with how lucky you are with the power of 2 which divides the number of commits between the last time hopscotch ran and the commit which deleted the module without deprecating or whatever.

I think it ends at reporting exactly the "last known good" and "first known bad" so that this is an implementation detail.

I was under the impression that it is guaranteed to point you to either the head commit, or a commit that breaks your repo, but the previous one didn't.

However, there is no actual guarantee that the commit that it points to is the first/last with this property.
Looking at the docs, I now remember that binary is the default but that there is also a linear search option, so you are usually right.

@Marcelo Lynch would it make sense to somehow indicate which PRs are the last PR in a bors batch, and only use those in the bisection steps?
And then we configure bors to add the deprecated modules PRs in the correct batch?

Damiano Testa said:

I was under the impression that it is guaranteed to point you to either the head commit, or a commit that breaks your repo, but the previous one didn't.

However, there is no actual guarantee that the commit that it points to is the first/last with this property.

This is correct. If there is a "bump interval" where you were (broken ... fixed ... broken again) you could land in either boundary depending on bisection "luck"
I thought this was a reasonable assumption but if this pattern is very common we can try to take it into account, especially if it's predictable like the case we're describing here

But note that if you are already "healthy" and you get broken by a module deprecation that will then be fixed "right away" in a few commits, the next hopscotch run should see that you've recovered and you're "okay" again, so you just need to wait

Johan Commelin said:

Marcelo Lynch would it make sense to somehow indicate which PRs are the last PR in a bors batch, and only use those in the bisection steps?
And then we configure bors to add the deprecated modules PRs in the correct batch?

I don't get it though, if these things can be batched together and one fixes the other, why is it not the same PR?
Bors creates one commit per PR
Because git doesn't track renames internally, it can only recover the fact that a file was renamed after the fact, commit-by-commit

Chris Henson said:

Jireh Loreaux said:

Anatole, it's been like 24 hours or something, so I wouldn't say that's your fault. The issue is that hopscotch is continually building against the latest Mathlib, whereas before we had a window (until the next monthly release) where downstream projects wouldn't be affected.

I think part of the issue is that a lot of downstream projects update Mathlib very frequently, use the release candidate toolchains, etc. (...)

Just to mention regarding this: it is my goal with the whole hospcotch business that everyone is trying to bump as often as possible, so this should be the norm and not the exception.

I personally think this sort of thing where we push a breaking change (that we intend to fix) willingly is a bit pathological, and we should try not to do it. If this 'git rename' thing is a hard requirement, then sure, let's accomodate for this scenario (probably with a combination of downstream-reports and bors logic to try to reduce + recognize this 'race').

But in my mind this is just 'choosing to do the wrong thing because it's convenient', and pushing a commit with breaking changes is commiting to breaking someone who happens to pick that commit to update. In other words (and again people might disagree with me here) I think that every commit to the master branch should be 'something that should be legitimately consumable' by downstreams.

I agree it's a bit weird, but I at the same time I think it's a bit weird to expect that anyone should be able to bump to any random commit of a project's master branch. Almost all software has releases.
Btw, I think that adding missing deprecations late is probably the most common explanation why a project may "heal" by just moving to a later commit.

Jireh Loreaux said:

We've been doing it to make the file movements easier to see in the git history, but at this point I'm a bit skeptical that it's worth the hassle.

Anatole Dedecker said:

A possible fix would be "we create the deprecation right before merging the PR" (automatically ? using a GitHub bot ?)

In the interest of making some concrete plans here to address the situation: while it would mess up tracking renames if you only looked at commits on master, would anyone be strongly opposed if we made a bot triggered by some command (!deprecated_module?) that looked for missing module deprecations on a PR branch, pushed a commit to the PR branch adding them, and then triggered bors on the PR? (Obviously we wouldn't deploy this bot all in one go, we'd have to do a lot of testing before enabling the last step.)

IIUC you mean we would no longer split the rename and deprecation into separate commits on master? If so then I would be strongly opposed.
I think looking through git history of a renamed file happens more often than files being deprecated.

Surely we could find a solution that works for both, such as in CI forcing PR descriptions of PRs that rename modules to contain deprecations for renamed modules: #12345 then Hopscotch could search for the matching commit (w/ message ending in (#12345)) and ignore the commit range between them.

If there's no matching commit it means the deprecations PR wasn't merged yet, and if at least a day passed then it's fair game for Hopscotch to bump and consider it a breaking change.

OK, I'm slightly concerned about adding more complexity to bors, but after thinking some more, it should be possible to add a feature to bors so that it merges the rename commit and deprecation commit together as separate commits. For example, we could have a command like bors merge2 <sha> where everything before <sha> on the PR branch gets squashed into one commit and then <sha> and everything afterwards gets squashed into another commit, and then both of those land on staging together. (I suppose we could even generalize this to n separate commits if we ever needed it.)

Would everyone be happy with that?

Note that the deprecated module linter is planned to be upstreamed: batteries#1803. The only planned behavior change is proposed at mathlib#39408 (mild but still waiting for acceptance). Please let me know how to cooperate with your changes.

I suspect merge2 would be too complicated to use, as it requires the contributor to understand git well enough to split the commits and force-push if they have to, and also the maintainer to remember to merge2 or for bors d+ to allow others to use merge2.
Also keeping it in the same PR means the diff will be hard to review, e.g. see Vertex.lean in #37546 which is a rename + adding deprecation.
But I'm not sure I have anything better to suggest sadly

Maybe:

  • Using CI require PRs with moves/deletions to contain deprecations: #12345
  • bors merge will merge both the current PR and the deprecations PR
Can we go further and make bors autogenerate the deprecation PR?

With merge2 I was thinking that eventually the workflow would be: the maintainer would approve a PR that just does the rename with a special command; then some other automation similar to what I described in my first message above (#mathlib4 > deprecated module @ 💬 ) would add the deprecation module, and it would then also automatically trigger bors with the precise merge2 syntax required.
There's a lot of moving parts there so we'd have to roll it out in pieces, of course.

I have been implementing some new bors commands to support better discipline in this scenario (and hopefully usable in other cases). The idea is to signal to bors that two PRs should be bundled together:

  • bors link #x on PR #y makes {x, y} a bundle that merges atomically: each PR is still reviewed and r+'d individually, and once the last one is approved they all enter the same batch, and merge together or not at all.
  • bors stack #x on #y is similar to link but imposes additional constraints: #y is merged right after #x, and is expected to have branched off #x (the stack command is refused unless #y contains #x's current head). This would be the case for module deprecations
This intentionally leaves any semantics beyond commit batching outside of bors -- we can impose additional verifications per-scenario if we want to really enforce that this happens in every case
